channel.title: GridDojo
channel.description: Clear, tested tutorials and honest comparisons for Excel and Google Sheets — so you can stop fighting your spreadsheet and get back to work.

item.title: How to Use INDEX MATCH in Excel (with Examples)
item.description: INDEX MATCH is the flexible lookup that fixes VLOOKUP's biggest limits — it can look to the left and it does not break when you add columns. Here is exactly how INDEX and MATCH work together, step by step.

item.title: How to Use COUNTIF in Excel (with Examples)
item.description: COUNTIF counts only the cells that meet a condition. The syntax is =COUNTIF(range, criteria) — like counting how many sales came from one region. Here is exactly how it works, plus wildcards, counting duplicates, and COUNTIFS.

item.title: How to Make a Budget in Google Sheets
item.description: To make a budget in Google Sheets, list your income and expenses, total each with SUM, subtract to find your balance, and group spending by category with SUMIF. Here is how to build a simple, free budget from scratch.

item.title: How to Sort and Filter Data in Google Sheets
item.description: To sort in Google Sheets, use Data > Sort range; to filter, use Data > Create a filter and pick which rows to show. Sorting reorders your data, filtering hides rows without deleting them. Here is how to do both, step by step.

item.title: How to Use Conditional Formatting in Google Sheets
item.description: Conditional formatting colors a cell automatically based on its value — to highlight, rank, or flag data. Select your cells, open Format > Conditional formatting, and set a rule. Here is how to use single-color rules, color scales, and custom formulas.

item.title: How to Use Conditional Formatting in Excel
item.description: Conditional formatting changes a cell's color automatically based on its value — to highlight, rank, or flag data. Select your cells, open Home > Conditional Formatting, and pick a rule. Here is how to use every type, step by step.

item.title: Apple Numbers vs Excel: Which Should You Use?
item.description: Apple Numbers is free, elegant, and great for Mac and iPhone users; Excel is the paid, cross-platform standard with far more power. Numbers suits simple, good-looking spreadsheets, Excel suits serious data work. Here is how they compare.

item.title: LibreOffice Calc vs Excel: Which Should You Use?
item.description: LibreOffice Calc is a free, open-source desktop spreadsheet; Excel is the paid industry standard with deeper features. Calc covers everyday work at no cost, Excel wins on power and compatibility. Here is how they compare.

item.title: How to Use SUMIF in Excel (with Examples)
item.description: SUMIF adds up only the numbers that meet a condition. The syntax is =SUMIF(range, criteria, [sum_range]) — like totaling sales for one region. Here is exactly how each part works, plus SUMIFS and wildcards.

item.title: Airtable vs Excel: Which Should You Use?
item.description: Excel is a true spreadsheet for calculations and analysis; Airtable is a database with spreadsheet looks, built for organizing and linking records. Use Excel for numbers, Airtable for structured data and workflows. Here is how they compare.

item.title: Microsoft 365 vs Google Workspace: Which Is Better?
item.description: Microsoft 365 gives you powerful desktop apps like Excel and works best offline; Google Workspace is built for real-time collaboration in the browser. Pick Microsoft for depth, Google for teamwork. Here is the full comparison.

item.title: How to Use SUMIF in Google Sheets
item.description: SUMIF adds up numbers that meet a condition. The syntax is =SUMIF(range, criterion, sum_range) — for example, total sales for one region. Here is exactly how each part works, with examples.

item.title: Notion vs Google Sheets: Which Should You Use?
item.description: Google Sheets is a true spreadsheet built for calculations and data; Notion is an all-in-one workspace with light databases. Use Sheets for numbers and analysis, Notion for notes, wikis, and tracking. Here is how they compare.

item.title: How to Fix the #NAME? Error in Excel
item.description: The #NAME? error means Excel does not recognize something in your formula — usually a misspelled function, missing quotation marks around text, or an unknown name. Here is how to find the cause and fix it.

item.title: How to Freeze Rows and Columns in Google Sheets
item.description: To freeze rows in Google Sheets, open the View menu, choose Freeze, and pick how many rows or columns to lock. They then stay visible as you scroll. Here is how to freeze, adjust, and unfreeze them.

item.title: How to Use the IF Function in Google Sheets
item.description: The IF function in Google Sheets returns one value when a condition is true and another when it is false. The syntax is =IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false). Here is exactly how each part works, with examples.

item.title: How to Fix the #DIV/0! Error in Excel
item.description: The #DIV/0! error means a formula is dividing by zero or by an empty cell. The fix is to correct the denominator, or wrap the formula in IFERROR or IF so it returns a blank or a message instead. Here is how.

item.title: How to Make a Drop-Down List in Google Sheets
item.description: To make a drop-down list in Google Sheets, select the cells, open Data > Data validation, add a rule with the Dropdown criteria, and enter your options. Here is how to build, edit, and troubleshoot one.

item.title: How to Make a Graph in Google Sheets
item.description: To make a graph in Google Sheets, select your data, click Insert > Chart, and pick a chart type in the Chart editor. Here is how to build it, choose the right type, and customize it — step by step.

item.title: How to Create a Drop-Down List in Excel
item.description: To create a drop-down list in Excel, select the cells, go to Data > Data Validation, choose Allow: List, and type your options or point to a range. Here is how to build, edit, and troubleshoot one.
